title: 00 - CFK Platform / Kubernetes Operations
description: Dashboard 1 of 3 (Platform -> Component -> Workload). Is Kubernetes/OpenShift infrastructure, scheduling, storage, networking, or an operator causing the problem? All panels use kube-state-metrics, kubelet/cAdvisor, and Prometheus self-metrics only for Layer 1A - no node-exporter is deployed in this single-node CRC lab (deliberately trimmed, see apps/observability-app.yaml), so node-level disk IOPS/latency are not available and are not faked here (federating an OpenShift-platform node-exporter was evaluated and documented as a P1 item in docs/observability/GAP-ANALYSIS.md, not silently dropped). Only the first three rows are expanded by default (golden signals, node health, pod table) - every other row is collapsed to keep the first viewport operational rather than a long scroll.

panels.title: Pod Status Distribution
panels.description:
WHAT: Current split of platform pods by phase.
WHY: One glance at the whole stack's health instead of three separate counters.
NORMAL: All Running (one wedge).
PROBLEM: Any Pending/Failed wedge appears.
NEXT: Pod Operational Table below to see which pod left Running.

panels.title: Cluster CPU: Requested vs Remaining
panels.description:
WHAT: This stack's CPU requests vs what's left of the cluster's allocatable CPU (single-node CRC lab, so cluster == node; see the per-node bar gauges in Node Health for the multi-node-portable version).
WHY: This CRC node has repeatedly hit >90% requested, causing liveness-probe timeouts across every pod (Grafana, Prometheus, Connect, Control Center all observed flapping under this condition).
NORMAL: Remaining wedge clearly visible.
PROBLEM: Remaining wedge near-zero -> scheduler starves even trivial health-check handlers.
NEXT: Reduce component resource requests, or raise CRC's `crc config set cpus/memory` allocation and restart CRC.

panels.title: Cluster Memory: Requested vs Remaining
panels.description:
WHAT: This stack's memory requests vs what's left of the cluster's allocatable memory.
WHY: Same overcommit risk as CPU - this node has been observed at 99-100% memory requests.
NORMAL: Remaining wedge clearly visible.
PROBLEM: Remaining wedge near-zero.
NEXT: Same remediation as Cluster CPU: Requested vs Remaining.

panels.title: Prometheus Targets: Up vs Down
panels.description:
WHAT: Every ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor target, split by whether the last scrape succeeded.
WHY: Distinguishes 'metric is really zero' from 'we have no data' across every other panel on this dashboard.
NORMAL: All Up (one wedge).
PROBLEM: Any Down wedge appears - a component's /metrics endpoint is unreachable (NetworkPolicy, pod down, port change).
NEXT: Prometheus Self-Monitoring row: check `up{job=...}` for the specific job, then NetworkPolicy/pod status.

panels.title: Container Restarts (1h)
panels.description:
WHAT: Container restarts in the last hour, platform-wide.
WHY: Restarts hide instability that 'pod is Running' alone won't show.
NORMAL: 0
PROBLEM: Any sustained increase
NEXT: Pod Operational Table -> Scheduling/Failures row for CrashLoopBackOff/OOMKilled reasons.

panels.title: Platform CPU usage vs allocatable
panels.description:
WHAT: Actual CPU usage vs requested vs the cluster's total allocatable CPU (cores).
WHY: No node-exporter is deployed here (single-node CRC lab, deliberately trimmed) so this is derived from kube-state-metrics + kubelet/cAdvisor, not node_cpu_seconds_total. See docs/observability/GAP-ANALYSIS.md for the node-exporter federation option evaluated for production.
NORMAL: usage line well under the allocatable line
PROBLEM: usage or requested approaching allocatable
NEXT: Namespace Capacity row to find which namespace is driving it.

panels.title: Node CPU: requested / allocatable %, by node

targets.expr: sum by (node) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu", namespace=~"$namespace"}) / on(node) max by (node) (kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="cpu"}) * 100

panels.description:
WHAT: Per-node CPU requested as a % of that node's allocatable - written to generalize cleanly to a real multi-node cluster (this CRC lab only has one node, 'crc', so it's a single bar today).
WHY: The multi-node-portable, ranked version of the cluster-wide allocation % pie above - on a real cluster this is where you'd spot one specific overloaded worker.
NORMAL: well under 70% for every node
PROBLEM: a specific node's bar much higher than its peers
NEXT: Reschedule/rebalance workloads off that node, or add capacity.

panels.title: Node Memory: requested / allocatable %, by node

targets.expr: sum by (node) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="memory", namespace=~"$namespace"}) / on(node) max by (node) (kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory"}) * 100

panels.description:
WHAT: Per-node memory requested as a % of that node's allocatable.
WHY: Same overcommit risk as CPU, ranked by node instead of summed cluster-wide.
NORMAL: well under 75% for every node
PROBLEM: a specific node's bar much higher than its peers
NEXT: Same remediation as Node CPU: requested / allocatable %.

panels.title: Node Conditions
panels.description:
WHAT: Current Kubernetes node conditions (Ready/MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure/NetworkUnavailable) with status=true.
WHY: A true MemoryPressure/DiskPressure condition means the kubelet itself is evicting pods, a step worse than plain overcommit.
NORMAL: Only condition=Ready
PROBLEM: Any of MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure/NetworkUnavailable present
NEXT: oc describe node crc

panels.title: Pod status / restarts / resource usage
panels.description:
WHAT: One row per pod: actual status (Running/Pending/Failed/Unknown - the phase label is now preserved, not dropped by an aggregation), restart count, CPU cores, memory bytes.
WHY: The single table an operator scans first when told 'something in the platform is unhealthy'.
NORMAL: phase=Running, restarts flat, cpu/mem well under limits (see Pod CPU/Pod Memory rows for the % view)
PROBLEM: phase != Running, or restarts climbing
NEXT: Open the pod's logs/events (oc logs / oc describe pod), or drill into the Pod CPU/Pod Memory rows for that pod's trend.

panels.title: Namespace Capacity
panels.description: CPU/memory usage vs requests vs limits, broken out per namespace.

panels.title: CPU: usage vs requests vs limits, by namespace
panels.description:
WHAT: Per-namespace CPU usage against what it asked for (requests) and its ceiling (limits). Requests are a scheduling reservation, not a runtime ceiling - usage running above requests is expected and not itself a problem.
WHY: A namespace whose usage tracks its limit line is the one starving everyone else; the request line is only useful context for scheduling headroom, not a health boundary.
NORMAL: usage comfortably under limits (usage vs requests can vary either way)
PROBLEM: usage approaching or exceeding limits
NEXT: Pod CPU row for per-pod limit%/throttling detail on the specific namespace.

panels.title: Memory: usage vs requests vs limits, by namespace
panels.description:
WHAT: Per-namespace memory usage against requests/limits. Requests are a scheduling reservation, not a runtime ceiling - usage above requests is normal and expected.
WHY: OOMKilled events happen when usage crosses the limit line, not the request line - that's the only line that matters for memory health.
NORMAL: usage comfortably under limits (usage vs requests can vary either way)
PROBLEM: usage approaching limits
NEXT: Kubernetes Scheduling/Failures row for OOMKilled detail on the specific pod.

panels.title: Pod CPU
panels.description: Per-pod CPU usage, limit ratio, and CFS throttling.

panels.title: CPU usage by pod, filtered by $component

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod", container!=""}[5m]) * on(pod) group_left() kube_pod_owner{owner_name=~"$component"})

panels.description:
WHAT: Per-pod CPU usage (cores), filterable by $component (the owning StatefulSet/Deployment - kafka, connect, schemaregistry, etc.) as well as $pod. The request line (see Namespace Capacity row) is a scheduling reservation, not a ceiling - running above it is normal.
WHY: Identifies which specific pod/component is consuming CPU.
NORMAL: Flat, well under its limit
PROBLEM: Sustained climb or spikes toward its limit
NEXT: CPU usage/limit %% and CPU throttling %% panels below.

panels.title: CPU usage / limit %, by pod

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod", container!=""}[5m])) / sum by (pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu", namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}) * 100

panels.description:
WHAT: CPU usage as a % of each pod's own CPU limit, ranked.
WHY: This is what actually triggers CFS throttling, not the node-wide %.
NORMAL: < 80%
PROBLEM: Sustained > 90-100%
NEXT: Consider raising the CR's podTemplate.resources.limits.cpu.

panels.title: CPU throttling %, by pod

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod", container!=""}[5m])) / sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod", container!=""}[5m])) * 100

panels.description:
WHAT: % of CFS scheduling periods where this container was throttled (hit its CPU limit and got paused mid-period), ranked across pods.
WHY: A pod can look fine on the plain CPU-usage graph while still being throttled - usage caps at the limit, throttling is what actually happens above it.
NORMAL: 0%
PROBLEM: Sustained > 10-25% - the pod is CPU-limited even though usage looks flat at the ceiling.
NEXT: Raise the CR's podTemplate.resources.limits.cpu, or investigate why that component needs more CPU than expected.

panels.title: Pod Memory
panels.description: Per-pod memory usage and limit ratio.

panels.title: Memory working set by pod
panels.description:
WHAT: Per-pod memory working set.
WHY: The number the kernel OOM-killer actually watches.
NORMAL: Flat, under limit
PROBLEM: Climbing toward the limit
NEXT: Memory usage/limit %% panel and OOMKilled panel below.

panels.title: Memory usage / limit %, by pod

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod", container!=""}) / sum by (pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory", namespace=~"$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}) * 100

panels.description:
WHAT: Memory usage as a % of each pod's own memory limit, ranked.
WHY: Crossing 100% here is an OOMKill, not a graceful slowdown like CPU throttling.
NORMAL: < 75%
PROBLEM: > 90%
NEXT: OOMKilled panel below; consider raising the CR's memory limit.

panels.title: Pod / Node Network
panels.description: Per-pod network throughput and errors/drops.

panels.title: RX/TX bytes/sec, by pod
panels.description:
WHAT: Network throughput per pod, from cAdvisor.
WHY: Kafka replication/produce traffic is the dominant load here.
NORMAL: Matches expected produce/consume/replication volume
PROBLEM: Sudden drop to zero (partition) or unexpected spike
NEXT: Cross-check against Dashboard 2 Kafka throughput panels for the same window.

panels.title: RX/TX errors and drops, by pod
panels.description:
WHAT: Network errors/drops per pod (cAdvisor container_network_* counters).
WHY: Distinguishes an application-level slowdown from an actual network/CNI problem.
NORMAL: 0
PROBLEM: > 0 sustained
NEXT: Check the OpenShift Control Plane & Network Fabric row for OVN health.

panels.title: Persistent Storage
panels.description: PVC utilization and growth trend.

panels.title: Storage: Used vs Free (all PVCs, $namespace)
panels.description:
WHAT: Aggregate used vs free bytes across every PVC in scope (kafka data0-*, kraftcontroller data0-*, controlcenter data0-*/prometheus-data-*, this stack's own Prometheus PVC).
WHY: One glance at overall storage headroom before drilling into which specific PVC is driving it.
NORMAL: Free wedge clearly visible.
PROBLEM: Free wedge near-zero.
NEXT: The per-PVC bar gauge below to find which specific volume is full.

panels.title: PVC utilization %, by volume
panels.description:
WHAT: PVC used/capacity, ranked per volume.
WHY: A full PVC on a Kafka broker stops it accepting writes.
NORMAL: < 70%
PROBLEM: > 85%
NEXT: The growth panel below to estimate days-to-full, then expand the PVC or trim retention.

panels.title: PVC growth (used bytes, 24h)
panels.description:
WHAT: Raw used-bytes trend per PVC over the selected window.
WHY: Slope of this line, projected forward, is the capacity-exhaustion estimate.
NORMAL: Flat or slow linear growth matching expected retention
PROBLEM: Steep/accelerating growth
NEXT: Check Kafka log retention settings (base/confluent-platform/kafka.yaml) or Prometheus retention (8h, deliberately short for this lab).

panels.title: Kubernetes Scheduling / Failures
panels.description: Pending/Failed pods, OOMKilled containers, waiting-state reasons.

panels.title: Pods: Running vs Not Running
panels.description:
WHAT: Any platform pod not in Running phase, as a share of the whole.
WHY: Single combined signal for scheduling/crash problems.
NORMAL: All Running (one wedge).
PROBLEM: Not Running wedge appears.
NEXT: Pod Operational Table above, then oc describe pod for the specific pod.

panels.title: OOMKilled containers (last-terminated)
panels.description:
WHAT: Containers whose most recent termination reason was OOMKilled.
WHY: Direct evidence the memory limit, not just the request, is too low.
NORMAL: 0
PROBLEM: > 0
NEXT: Raise the CR's podTemplate.resources.limits.memory for that component.

panels.title: Waiting-state containers, by reason (CrashLoopBackOff / ImagePullBackOff / etc.)
panels.description:
WHAT: Containers currently stuck in a Waiting state, labeled by reason.
WHY: CrashLoopBackOff/ImagePullBackOff are the two most common blockers on a fresh CRC boot.
NORMAL: No series (nothing waiting)
PROBLEM: Any series present
NEXT: oc describe pod for the exact reason/message.

panels.title: StatefulSet / Deployment Health
panels.description: Desired-vs-ready replica convergence for every Confluent StatefulSet and operator Deployment.

panels.title: Confluent StatefulSets: ready / desired %
panels.description:
WHAT: Ready replicas as a % of desired, per StatefulSet (kafka, kraftcontroller, connect, schemaregistry, controlcenter, kafkarestproxy).
WHY: CFK manages every Confluent component as a StatefulSet - this is the CR-level health signal, distinct from pod-level status.
NORMAL: 100% for all six
PROBLEM: < 100% sustained
NEXT: oc get pods -n confluent -l app=<component>; check the CFK operator's own logs.

panels.title: Operators and Flink job: ready / desired %
panels.description:
WHAT: Ready replicas as a % of desired, per Deployment - the CFK operator, Flink Kubernetes operator, CMF operator, and the Flink job's own Deployment (statefarm-claims-processor).
WHY: A ready operator pod does NOT mean the CRs it manages are healthy - see Dashboard 2 for actual Kafka/Connect/etc. health.
NORMAL: 100% for all
PROBLEM: < 100%
NEXT: oc get pods -n <operator-namespace>; oc logs on the operator pod.

panels.title: Prometheus Self-Monitoring
panels.description: Target scrape health, scrape duration, and rule-evaluation failures.

panels.title: Scrape targets (up=1/0 by job)
panels.description:
WHAT: Every ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor target Prometheus knows about, and whether the last scrape succeeded.
WHY: This is what separates 'the metric is really zero' from 'Prometheus can't reach the target at all' throughout every other dashboard here.
NORMAL: All rows = 1
PROBLEM: Any row = 0
NEXT: Check the target's NetworkPolicy (see bootstrap/network-policies.yaml's monitoring-scrape-confluent rule) and pod status.

panels.title: Scrape duration by job
panels.description:
WHAT: How long each scrape took.
WHY: A slow scrape under node CPU pressure is an early warning before a target starts timing out entirely.
NORMAL: Well under the scrape interval (30s)
PROBLEM: Approaching or exceeding the interval
NEXT: Correlate with Node Health's Cluster CPU allocation %% panel.

panels.title: Rule evaluation failures
panels.description:
WHAT: PrometheusRule (recording/alerting) evaluations that failed.
WHY: A silent failure here means recording rules and alerts in base/observability/rules stop updating without any obvious symptom.
NORMAL: 0
PROBLEM: > 0
NEXT: oc logs on the Prometheus pod for the specific rule group error.

panels.title: OpenShift Security / Platform State
panels.description: cert-manager certificate expiry tracking.

panels.title: TLS certificate days remaining (cert-manager issued)
panels.description:
WHAT: Days until each cert-manager-issued certificate expires (platform-ca-issuer chain, plus every operator's self-signed serving cert - Flink operator, CMF, etc.), ranked worst-first.
WHY: An expired cert silently breaks TLS-dependent internal traffic (Kafka listeners, Argo CD, webhooks) with no other obvious symptom.
NORMAL: > 30 days remaining for every cert, decreasing linearly then jumping back up on cert-manager's automatic renewal.
PROBLEM: < 14 days remaining and NOT renewing (a flat/non-renewing bar close to 0).
NEXT: oc describe certificate -A for the specific cert; check cert-manager pod logs for renewal failures.

panels.title: OpenShift Control Plane & Network Fabric (Layer 1B)
panels.description: Unlocked via the observability-prometheus ServiceAccount's system:monitoring ClusterRole binding (see platform-metrics-rbac.yaml) - these endpoints are gated behind kube-rbac-proxy and were unreachable before that grant. etcd is NOT included: confirmed it additionally requires a client certificate beyond the bearer token. ClusterOperator/ClusterVersion/MachineConfigPool status, admission-webhook latency, and CSI health are further P1 items - see docs/observability/GAP-ANALYSIS.md.

panels.title: kube-apiserver: request error rate (5xx)
panels.description:
WHAT: % of kube-apiserver requests returning a 5xx error.
WHY: apiserver errors cascade into every controller/operator in the cluster (CFK operator, ArgoCD, Flink operator).
NORMAL: ~0%
PROBLEM: sustained >1-5%
NEXT: oc get --raw /healthz on the apiserver; check node resource pressure (Node Health row).

panels.title: kube-apiserver: P99 request latency (overall)
panels.description:
WHAT: P99 latency across ALL kube-apiserver requests, regardless of verb/resource.
WHY: The single-number headline; see the by-verb breakdown below to find which request type is actually slow.
NORMAL: well under 1s on a healthy cluster
PROBLEM: climbing toward multiple seconds - every oc/kubectl command and controller reconcile loop slows down with it.
NEXT: the by-verb/resource panels below.

panels.title: kube-scheduler: pending pods
panels.description:
WHAT: Pods waiting to be scheduled.
WHY: NORMAL: 0, or briefly >0 during a rollout.
NORMAL: 0
PROBLEM: sustained >0 - insufficient node capacity or an unsatisfiable scheduling constraint.
NEXT: Kubernetes Scheduling/Failures row.

panels.title: CoreDNS: error response ratio
panels.description:
WHAT: % of DNS responses that are NOT NOERROR (SERVFAIL/NXDOMAIN/REFUSED), as a ratio of total responses - not a raw rate, so it distinguishes '17 errors out of 20 requests' from '17 out of 200,000'.
WHY: Broken DNS breaks every Kafka/Connect/SR hostname resolution in the cluster silently.
NORMAL: low - a nonzero NXDOMAIN ratio for genuinely nonexistent names is normal at low volume
PROBLEM: a high/climbing SERVFAIL-driven ratio
NEXT: the rcode breakdown panel below, then oc logs -n openshift-dns.

panels.title: kube-apiserver: P99 latency by verb
panels.description: WHAT: P99 latency broken out by verb (GET/LIST/WATCH/CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE) - the overall P99 stat above hides which specific request type is slow. WHY: a LIST or WATCH spike often points at a controller doing an expensive full-resync. NORMAL: sub-second for all verbs. PROBLEM: one verb's P99 climbing while others stay flat.

panels.title: kube-apiserver: request rate by verb
panels.description: WHAT: apiserver request volume by verb. WHY: correlate a rate spike in a verb against that same verb's P99 latency panel to see if volume is causing the slowdown.

panels.title: CoreDNS: request rate & response breakdown by rcode
panels.description: WHAT: overall DNS query volume plus the response-code breakdown (NOERROR/NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL/REFUSED) the error-ratio stat above is derived from. WHY: a spike in requests often correlates with a CrashLoopBackOff pod repeatedly re-resolving on every restart; a spike in a specific rcode pinpoints which failure mode.

panels.title: CoreDNS: P99 request duration
panels.description: WHAT: P99 time CoreDNS takes to answer a query. NORMAL: low milliseconds. PROBLEM: climbing - every service-name lookup in the cluster gets slower, including Kafka/Connect/SR's own internal hostname resolution.

panels.title: kube-scheduler: scheduling attempts & algorithm duration (P99)
panels.description: WHAT: rate of scheduling attempts and how long the scheduling algorithm itself takes per attempt. WHY: a high attempt rate with pods still Pending (see stat panel above) plus climbing algorithm duration means the scheduler is both busy and slow to place them.

panels.title: OVN-Kubernetes node: CNI setup latency & workqueue depth
panels.description: WHAT: how long OVN takes to wire up networking for a new pod (CNI ADD), and its internal controller's backlog. WHY: this is the 'why is my pod stuck ContainerCreating' signal. NORMAL: sub-second CNI setup, workqueue depth near 0. PROBLEM: CNI setup climbing into seconds, or a growing workqueue depth - the node's OVN controller is falling behind.
